title: Capstone: RGB Color Packer
description:
Pack and unpack colours like a graphics engine does.
```
Enter R G B (0-255): 255 136 0
Packed:  0xFF8800  (16746496)
Binary:  00000000111111111000100000000000
Unpacked: R=255 G=136 B=0
Inverted: 0x0077FF
Grayscale value: 156
Brightened 20%: R=255 G=163 B=0
```
hints: Read the numbers into `int`s, not `std::uint8_t`: a `std::uint8_t` is a character type, so `std::cin` would read one character instead of a number (lesson 2.04).
The colour sits in the low 24 bits: red is bits 16–23, green 8–15, blue 0–7. Shift the part you want down to the bottom, then `& 0xFF` keeps just those 8 bits.

Inverting flips every bit, including the 8 unused ones at the top, so mask them away: `~packed & 0xFFFFFF`. For "brightened 20%", work in `int`, multiply by 1.2, and keep it at most 255 with `std::min(255, value)`.

The starter's print line uses three switches that change how `std::cout` prints integers from then on: `std::hex` (base 16), `std::uppercase` (`FF`, not `ff`) and `std::dec` (back to base 10). Hex prints no leading zeros, so for `0x0077FF` pad to six digits with `<iomanip>`:

```cpp
std::cout << std::hex << std::uppercase << std::setfill('0') << std::setw(6) << 0x77FF << std::dec << std::setfill(' ');   // 0077FF
```
requirements: `std::uint32_t pack(std::uint8_t r, std::uint8_t g, std::uint8_t b)` using `<<` and `|`
Print hex with `std::hex << std::uppercase` (see the last hint)
